analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse-to-patient staffing ratios in hospitals and protects nurses who object to unsafe assignments.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Senator Barbara Boxer with 4 cosponsors in March 2015, never received a committee hearing or vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital to follow minimum registered-nurse-to-patient ratios by unit — for example, one nurse for every four patients in a medical-surgical unit — with no averaging across shifts and no mandatory overtime to cover shortfalls. It would have let nurses refuse assignments that violate the ratios or that they are not trained for, protected them from being fired or reported to licensing boards for doing so, and created a toll-free hotline patients could call to report understaffing. It would also have adjusted Medicare payments to hospitals to help cover the added cost, and added scholarships and mentorship grants to grow the nursing workforce.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who would be cared for under guaranteed staffing levels tied to patient safety; registered nurses, who would gain enforceable staffing standards, the right to refuse unsafe assignments without retaliation, and a federal whistleblower cause of action; and nursing students, who would be eligible for new stipends and mentorship grants.

how_it_helps.text: Requires hospitals to implement staffing plans with minimum direct-care RN-to-patient ratios by unit, such as 1:2 in intensive care, 1:3 in emergency rooms, and 1:4 in medical-surgical units [S2] [S3].
Bars hospitals from averaging staffing across shifts or using mandatory overtime to meet the ratios, and requires that only a direct-care registered nurse relieve another nurse during breaks [S3].

Gives nurses the right to refuse assignments that violate the ratios or that they are not qualified for, and prohibits hospitals from firing, discriminating against, or reporting such nurses to state licensing boards, with a federal court remedy including reinstatement and lost wages [S2] [S3].
Requires hospitals to post actual staffing ratios in each unit, keep records open to nurses and the public, and provides a toll-free hotline patients can use to report inadequate staffing [S3].

Directs HHS to adjust Medicare payments to cover hospitals' added costs of compliance, and expands nurse scholarship stipends and nurse retention, preceptorship, and mentorship grants to build the workforce [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals would bear the cost of hiring enough nurses to meet the ratios, ban on averaging, ban on mandatory overtime, and civil penalties of up to $25,000 per knowing violation. Medicare would cover the added cost of treating Medicare beneficiaries, meaning federal taxpayers would absorb part of the bill; costs of caring for privately insured patients would otherwise be absorbed by hospitals or passed through to insurers and premiums. Rural hospitals would get a longer phase-in of up to four years, an acknowledgment that the nurse supply is tight.

drawbacks.text: Compliance would require hiring many additional registered nurses, and hospitals argued such mandates raise labor costs significantly; the bill itself anticipates the burden by letting MedPAC estimate total costs and savings and adjusting Medicare payments accordingly, which shifts part of the cost to federal taxpayers [S3].

With a national nursing shortage, an immediate mandate could leave hospitals without enough nurses to fill the ratios; the bill responds with up to four-year phase-ins for rural hospitals, new scholarships, and mentorship grants, but a gap between the mandate and the workforce could strain smaller facilities [S3].

Fixed unit-by-unit ratios give hospitals less flexibility than purely acuity-based staffing systems; the bill addresses this by requiring staffing above the minimums based on patient acuity, but it does not allow any unit to fall below the fixed minimums [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-safety and nurse-protection gains are substantial and direct, and the bill anticipates its own costs: it phases in over two to four years, covers Medicare's share of added hospital costs, and funds nursing scholarships and mentorships to grow the supply. The real weaknesses are the transition risk while the nurse workforce expands and the fact that taxpayers fund part of the hospital cost. On balance it is a carefully structured response to a known patient-safety problem rather than an unfunded mandate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on March 25, 2015, joined by Senator Sherrod Brown [S3] [S5].
Four senators cosponsored the bill: three Democrats and one Independent [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; that was its only action [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals were better off because the bill never moved: they avoided a federal staffing ratio mandate, its hiring costs, and civil penalties. Nurses and hospital patients, who the bill was written for, received nothing.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to establish federal hospital nurse staffing ratios and nurse whistleblower protections

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: Original cosponsor (bill introduced 'for herself and Mr. Brown')

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican majority, chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — allowing it to expire at the end of the Congress

against.name: Hospital industry groups
against.what_they_did: Long publicly opposed federal nurse-to-patient ratio mandates as costly and inflexible staffing requirements

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent who caucuses with Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the Republican-led committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill would force hospitals to hire enough registered nurses to meet fixed per-unit ratios, ban averaging and mandatory overtime to cover shortfalls, and expose them to penalties up to $25,000 per knowing violation, with staffing records open to public inspection. Hospitals would lose staffing flexibility they use to control labor costs — the very flexibility that produces understaffing patients experience.

Nurses would gain enforceable staffing standards, the right to refuse unsafe assignments without retaliation, a federal court cause of action with reinstatement and back pay, and protected rights to organize. Their interest here runs alongside patient safety, since ratios tie nurse workload to patient care.

industries.industry: Nursing schools and workforce grant programs
industries.note: The bill adds stipends to the nurse scholarship and loan repayment program and expands retention grants to fund preceptorship and mentorship projects, directing money into training the expanded workforce the ratios require.
